title: The Smartphone
tagline: From brick-sized car phones to a supercomputer in every pocket
intro: Look around: there is probably a smartphone within arm's reach right now. It is a telephone, a camera, a map, a music player, a game console, a library and a flashlight, all squeezed into a slab of glass thinner than a pencil. But fifty years ago, a 'mobile phone' meant a heavy radio bolted into the trunk of a car! In these 20 parts we will travel from Alexander Graham Bell's wires and the first car phones to Martin Cooper's famous street-corner call in 1973, through chunky 'brick' phones, the first text message, pocket organizers, the forgotten IBM Simon, BlackBerry's keyboards, the iPhone and Android. Then we will open the phone up and see how touchscreens, chips, radio networks, batteries, cameras and sensors really work. Finally we will explore apps, how phones changed the whole world, the problems they cause, and where they might go next. Ready? Let's dial in.

outline.title: Talking Without Wires: The World Before Mobile Phones
covers: Alexander Graham Bell's telephone patent (1876): calls needed wires, so a phone was stuck to a wall or desk
Guglielmo Marconi and radio in the 1890s–1900s: sending messages through the air without wires

Two-way radios for police, ships and soldiers; the WWII Motorola 'Handie-Talkie' and 'walkie-talkie' radios (mention that several inventors, such as Al Gross and Donald Hings, have rival claims to the walkie-talkie)

The first public car phone service: AT&T's Mobile Telephone Service in St. Louis, June 17, 1946 — equipment weighing about 36 kg (80 lb), calls placed through a human operator, only a handful of channels so people waited in line
Why early car phones couldn't grow: one big transmitter per city meant very few people could call at the same time
Science fiction dreams: Dick Tracy's 2-Way Wrist Radio comic (1946) and the Star Trek communicator (1966)
keyFacts: Bell's telephone patent was granted in March 1876.
AT&T's Mobile Telephone Service began in St. Louis on June 17, 1946.
Early car phone equipment weighed about 36 kg (80 lb) and filled much of a car trunk.
In some cities hundreds of people were on waiting lists for a car phone because there were so few channels.
outline.hook: End with the big problem — too many people and too few radio channels — and tease that a clever idea about 'cells' would solve it.

outline.title: The First Handheld Call
covers: The cellular idea: Bell Labs engineers Douglas Ring and W. Rae Young described dividing a city into small 'cells' in a 1947 memo; the technology to build it took decades (keep the explanation short — Part 12 explains cells in depth)
The race between AT&T/Bell Labs (who imagined car phones) and Motorola (who wanted a phone you could carry)
Martin Cooper of Motorola makes the first public handheld cellular phone call on April 3, 1973, on a New York street, calling rival Joel Engel at Bell Labs
The prototype DynaTAC: about 1.1 kg (2.5 lb), around 20–30 minutes of talking and about 10 hours to recharge
The first commercial cellular networks: NTT in Tokyo (1979), Nordic NMT (1981), and Ameritech's AMPS network in Chicago (October 1983)
The Motorola DynaTAC 8000X goes on sale in 1983–84 for $3,995 — nicknamed 'the brick'
keyFacts: Martin Cooper's famous call was made on April 3, 1973, in New York City.
The DynaTAC 8000X weighed about 790 g (1.75 lb), was about 25 cm (10 inches) tall, and gave about 30 minutes of talk time.
It cost $3,995 in 1984 — roughly $12,000 in today's money.
Japan's NTT launched the world's first commercial cellular network in Tokyo in 1979.
outline.hook: End with the brick phone as a status symbol for the rich and tease that the next 15 years would make phones small, cheap and able to send words, not just voices.

outline.title: Phones Shrink and Learn to Text
covers: 1G vs 2G: first-generation phones sent voices as analog radio waves; second-generation (2G) phones turned voices into digital numbers
GSM, the European digital standard: first GSM call in Finland on July 1, 1991; the SIM card that holds your phone account
The first text message (SMS): 'Merry Christmas', sent by engineer Neil Papworth from a computer to a phone on December 3, 1992
Texting on number keys (pressing 7 four times for 'S') and predictive text like T9
Famous phones: Motorola StarTAC (1996) flip phone, Nokia 6110 with the game Snake (1997, by Taneli Armanto), Nokia 3310 (2000)
Ringtones, changeable covers and phones becoming personal style for teenagers
keyFacts: The world's first GSM call was made in Finland on July 1, 1991, on the Radiolinja network.
The first SMS, 'Merry Christmas', was sent on December 3, 1992, in the UK.
SMS messages were limited to 160 characters.
The Nokia 3310 (2000) sold well over 100 million units.
outline.hook: End by noting that phones could now talk and text, but people also wanted a pocket computer — and a different family of gadgets was growing up at the same time.

outline.title: Pocket Computers: The PDA
covers: What a PDA (personal digital assistant) was: an electronic organizer for calendars, contacts and notes — with no phone inside
The Psion Organiser (1984), often called the first PDA
Apple's Newton MessagePad (1993): Apple boss John Sculley popularized the term 'PDA'; its handwriting recognition was famously mocked, and it was discontinued in 1998
Palm Pilot (1996): Jeff Hawkins carried a wooden block in his shirt pocket to test the size; Graffiti, a simplified alphabet you wrote with a stylus
Syncing with a desktop computer through a cradle; Windows CE / Pocket PC devices as rivals
The idea of 'convergence': people carried a phone AND a PDA AND maybe a camera and an MP3 player — why not combine them?
keyFacts: The Psion Organiser was launched in 1984.
The Apple Newton MessagePad went on sale in 1993 for about $699.
The first Palm Pilot (1996) cost about $299 and was a big hit.
Graffiti used a single-stroke alphabet so the computer could recognize letters more easily.
outline.hook: End with the question: who would be first to put a PDA and a phone into one device? Tease that the answer came from IBM, surprisingly early.

outline.title: IBM Simon: The Forgotten First Smartphone
covers: IBM engineer Frank Canova and team; a prototype shown at the COMDEX computer show in November 1992
The IBM Simon Personal Communicator goes on sale through BellSouth in August 1994: touchscreen with a stylus, calendar, address book, notes, email, fax and even a sketch pad
Its problems: about $899 with a contract, about 500 g, a battery that lasted only around an hour of talk, and few buyers (about 50,000 sold)
Fair credit: Simon is widely called the first smartphone today, but the word 'smartphone' was not used for it at the time

Other early 'smart' phones: the Nokia 9000 Communicator (1996) with a keyboard that folded open; Ericsson's R380 (2000) marketed as a 'smartphone'; Symbian, the operating system shared by Nokia, Ericsson and others
Lesson: being first does not always mean being successful — timing, price and networks matter
keyFacts: IBM Simon went on sale in August 1994 for about $899 with a two-year contract.
Roughly 50,000 Simons were sold before it was withdrawn in 1995.
The Nokia 9000 Communicator was released in 1996.
Simon had no web browser; mobile networks were too slow and the web was very young.
outline.hook: End by asking where the mobile internet would really take off first — and reveal it was not America or Europe, but Japan.

outline.title: Japan's Mobile Internet Leap
covers: NTT Docomo's i-mode service (February 1999): email, news, weather, games and shopping on a phone — millions of users within a couple of years; Mari Matsunaga and Takeshi Natsuno helped shape it
Emoji: Shigetaka Kurita designed a famous set of 176 emoji for i-mode in 1999 (note that phone company J-Phone had an earlier, smaller set in 1997)
Camera phones: Kyocera VP-210 (1999) and the Sharp J-SH04 (2000) from J-Phone; sharing photos by email ('sha-mail')
World's first 3G network: Docomo's FOMA (2001) for faster data and video calls
Paying with your phone: 'Osaifu-Keitai' (wallet phone) using FeliCa chips from 2004
Why Japan's phones were advanced but stayed mostly inside Japan (the 'Galápagos' nickname)
keyFacts: NTT Docomo launched i-mode in February 1999.
The Sharp J-SH04, sold in Japan from late 2000, had a camera of about 0.11 megapixels.
NTT Docomo launched the world's first commercial 3G service, FOMA, in October 2001.
Emoji were added to the Unicode standard in 2010, which helped them spread worldwide.
outline.hook: End by switching to North America, where busy office workers were becoming addicted to a little device with a tiny keyboard.

outline.title: BlackBerry and the Keyboard Years
covers: Research In Motion (RIM), founded in Waterloo, Canada, in 1984 by Mike Lazaridis and Douglas Fregin; Jim Balsillie joins as co-leader
The BlackBerry 850 (1999), a two-way pager with a thumb keyboard and 'push' email that arrived instantly
BlackBerry phones in the 2000s: trackball/trackwheel, strong security, BlackBerry Messenger (BBM); the nickname 'CrackBerry'
Barack Obama insisting on keeping a (specially secured) BlackBerry as US President in 2009
Rivals: Palm/Handspring Treo, Windows Mobile phones, Nokia's Symbian smartphones (Nokia was the world's biggest phone maker)
Phones of the mid-2000s: tiny screens, physical keyboards, styluses, slow mobile web pages; the thin Motorola Razr (2004) as a fashion hit
keyFacts: RIM was founded in 1984 in Waterloo, Ontario, Canada.
The first BlackBerry device, the 850, launched in 1999.
BlackBerry reached roughly 80 million users at its peak in the early 2010s.
Nokia was the world's largest mobile phone maker from 1998 until about 2012.
outline.hook: End in 2006–2007: BlackBerry and Nokia feel unbeatable, while inside Apple a secret team is building something without a keyboard.

outline.title: One More Thing: The iPhone
covers: Apple's secret 'Project Purple'; Steve Jobs, designer Jony Ive, hardware leader Tony Fadell, software leader Scott Forstall; Apple had earlier bought FingerWorks, a multi-touch company
The Gorilla Glass story: Jobs asked Corning (CEO Wendell Weeks) for tough glass; Corning revived a 1960s experiment called 'Chemcor' and made it in months
The keynote on January 9, 2007: 'an iPod, a phone, and an internet communicator' — one device
What was new: a big multi-touch screen, pinch-to-zoom, a full web browser, no physical keyboard
What was missing: no 3G, no App Store, no copy-and-paste, a 2-megapixel camera with no video
Launch on June 29, 2007; rivals' reactions; the iPhone 3G and App Store in July 2008 (apps get their own part, Part 16)
keyFacts: Steve Jobs announced the iPhone at Macworld on January 9, 2007.
It went on sale in the US on June 29, 2007, at $499 (4 GB) and $599 (8 GB).
Its screen was 3.5 inches with 320 × 480 pixels.
Apple sold about 6 million first-generation iPhones.
outline.hook: End by revealing that Google had quietly bought a small startup years earlier — and its phone software was about to change direction because of the iPhone.

outline.title: Android and the Phone Wars
covers: Android Inc. founded in 2003 by Andy Rubin, Rich Miner, Nick Sears and Chris White; bought by Google in 2005
The Open Handset Alliance (November 2007): Android as free, open-source software built on Linux that many phone makers could use
The first Android phone: HTC Dream / T-Mobile G1 (October 2008), with a slide-out keyboard
Samsung's Galaxy phones (from 2010), big-screen 'phablets' like the Galaxy Note (2011), and cheaper Android phones from many companies, including in China and India
The patent wars: Apple v. Samsung (2011, settled 2018)

Winners and losers: Android becomes the most-used phone software; BlackBerry and Nokia fall behind (Nokia sells its phone business to Microsoft in 2014; BlackBerry stops designing its own phones in 2016)
keyFacts: Google bought Android Inc. in 2005.
The T-Mobile G1 / HTC Dream went on sale in the US in October 2008.
Today about 70% of the world's smartphones run Android, and most of the rest run Apple's iOS.
In 2012 a US jury awarded Apple about $1 billion against Samsung, later reduced; the companies settled in 2018.
outline.hook: End by saying it's time to open up the phone itself — starting with the part you touch hundreds of times a day: the screen.

outline.title: How It Works: Touchscreens and Displays
covers: E. A. Johnson's capacitive touchscreen at the UK's Royal Radar Establishment (described in 1965), used for air traffic control
Resistive touchscreens: G. Samuel Hurst's work in the 1970s (Elographics) — two layers pressed together; why they worked with styluses
How capacitive screens work: a grid of tiny invisible electrodes; your finger conducts electricity and changes the electric field, so the phone knows where you touched (why gloves don't work)
Multi-touch history: University of Toronto research (1982), Bill Buxton, FingerWorks, Jeff Han's 2006 demo
The display under the glass: pixels made of red, green and blue sub-pixels; LCD (needs a backlight) vs OLED (each pixel makes its own light)
Strong glass: ion exchange — big potassium ions squeezed into the glass surface make it harder to crack
keyFacts: E. A. Johnson published his capacitive touchscreen idea in 1965.
G. Samuel Hurst founded Elographics in 1971.
Modern phone screens often have more than 400 pixels per inch.
Capacitive touchscreens can sense many fingers at once; most resistive screens sense only one point.
outline.hook: End by asking: when you tap the screen, what actually decides what happens next? Lead into the chip, the phone's brain.

outline.title: How It Works: The Chip — A Brain Made of Sand
covers: Transistors as tiny on/off switches; silicon comes from sand; the transistor (1947) and the integrated circuit (late 1950s) in one short paragraph
Moore's Law: Gordon Moore's 1965 prediction that the number of transistors on chips would keep doubling (about every two years)
ARM: designed at Acorn in Britain by Sophie Wilson and Steve Furber (first chip 1985); ARM's power-saving designs are used in almost every smartphone
System-on-a-chip: CPU, graphics (GPU), AI engine (NPU), image processor and modem on one small chip
Comparison: the Apollo Guidance Computer (1969) vs a modern phone chip
Heat and battery: why phone chips must be efficient, not just fast
keyFacts: The first ARM chip ran in April 1985.
Apple's A17 Pro chip (2023) has about 19 billion transistors.
The Apollo Guidance Computer had about 4 kilobytes of changeable memory; a modern phone has billions of bytes.
Chip features are now just a few nanometers across — thousands of times thinner than a human hair.
outline.hook: End by noting that a brilliant brain is useless if it can't talk to the world — lead into invisible radio waves and phone networks.

outline.title: How It Works: Radio Waves, Cells and Networks
covers: Your voice and data become radio waves; frequencies and wavelengths explained simply
How cells work: each tower covers a small area; frequencies are reused in cells that aren't next to each other; 'handoff' passes your call from tower to tower as you move
The generations: 1G analog (1979–80s), 2G digital (1991), 3G mobile internet (2001), 4G LTE fast data (first network in Stockholm and Oslo, December 2009), 5G (2019)
The SIM card and how the network knows who you are
Wi-Fi (standard from 1997) and Bluetooth (Ericsson's Jaap Haartsen, named after the Viking-era king Harald Bluetooth)
Hedy Lamarr and George Antheil's 1942 frequency-hopping patent — an early idea related to later spread-spectrum radio (but do not say she invented Wi-Fi)
keyFacts: The first commercial 4G LTE networks opened in Stockholm and Oslo in December 2009.
South Korea and the US launched the first 5G phone services in April 2019.
Radio waves travel at the speed of light, about 300,000 km per second.
The Bluetooth industry group was formed in 1998.
outline.hook: End by pointing out that all this radio, computing and screen-glowing needs energy — so where does the phone get its power?

outline.title: How It Works: Batteries and Power
covers: How a battery works: chemical energy turns into electricity as lithium ions move between two electrodes
The lithium-ion battery: M. Stanley Whittingham (1970s), John Goodenough (cobalt oxide cathode, 1980), Akira Yoshino (first practical design, 1985); they shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry
Sony sold the first commercial lithium-ion batteries in 1991
Why batteries slowly wear out: charge cycles, heat, and capacity measured in mAh
Safety: the Samsung Galaxy Note 7 recall (2016) because of faulty batteries; why you shouldn't use damaged batteries
Saving power: dark modes on OLED screens, low-power chips, fast and wireless charging; the EU's USB-C common charger rule (from 2024)
keyFacts: Whittingham, Goodenough and Yoshino won the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for lithium-ion batteries.
Sony released the first commercial lithium-ion battery in 1991.
John Goodenough was 97 when he won the Nobel Prize, the oldest winner ever.
Samsung recalled and then stopped making the Galaxy Note 7 in 2016.
outline.hook: End by turning to the feature many people use more than calling: the camera.

outline.title: How It Works: The Camera in Your Pocket
covers: Light, lenses and focus explained simply; why phone lenses are so tiny

Image sensors: the CCD (Willard Boyle and George Smith at Bell Labs, 1969; Nobel Prize in Physics 2009) and the CMOS active-pixel sensor (Eric Fossum's team at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, early 1990s), which uses little power and is used in phones
Pixels and megapixels; why more megapixels does not always mean a better photo
Computational photography: the phone takes several pictures and combines them — HDR, night mode, portrait blur
Multiple lenses (wide, ultra-wide, zoom), image stabilization, video, front 'selfie' cameras
Brief look back: Philippe Kahn sharing a photo of his newborn daughter from a phone setup in 1997, and early camera phones (Part 6)
keyFacts: Boyle and Smith invented the CCD at Bell Labs in 1969 and shared part of the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Early camera phones (1999–2000) had about 0.1 megapixels; many modern phones have 12–200 megapixels.
The iPhone 4 (2010) was one of the first popular phones with a front-facing camera for video calls.
Phone cameras are now the most common cameras in the world; standalone camera sales have fallen sharply since about 2010.
outline.hook: End by revealing that the camera is only one of many 'senses' a phone has — it can also feel tilt, know its location, and recognize your face.

outline.title: How It Works: Sensors and GPS
covers: MEMS sensors: microscopic machines carved into silicon; the accelerometer (screen rotation, step counting) and gyroscope (turning, games)
Magnetometer (compass), barometer (height), proximity sensor (turns the screen off near your ear), ambient light sensor (brightness)

GPS: a US system of about 30 satellites; your phone measures how long signals take to arrive from at least four satellites; clocks must even be corrected for Einstein's relativity; other systems: Galileo, GLONASS, BeiDou
GPS people: Bradford Parkinson led the program; Gladys West's mathematical work on modeling Earth's shape helped make it accurate
Biometrics: fingerprint readers (Touch ID, 2013) and face unlocking with infrared dots (Face ID, 2017)
Sensors working together: maps, fitness trackers, emergency crash/fall detection
keyFacts: GPS satellites orbit about 20,200 km above Earth.
Without relativity corrections, GPS clocks would drift by about 38 microseconds a day, causing position errors of kilometers.
The US turned off the deliberate scrambling of civilian GPS ('Selective Availability') in May 2000, making it much more accurate.
Apple introduced Touch ID on the iPhone 5s in 2013 and Face ID on the iPhone X in 2017.
outline.hook: End by saying the hardware is amazing, but what made people fall in love with smartphones was software — apps.

outline.title: There's an App for That
covers: Apple's App Store opens on July 10, 2008, with about 500 apps; Android Market (2008), renamed Google Play in 2012
Anyone, even teenagers, could make and sell an app; how developers and app stores share money
Famous apps that changed habits: Angry Birds (2009), WhatsApp (2009), Instagram (2010), maps and navigation, ride-hailing (Uber), Pokémon Go (2016)
Mobile money: M-Pesa in Kenya (2007) let people send money by text, even on basic phones; tap-to-pay wallets like Apple Pay (2014)
App store rules and arguments: who decides which apps are allowed, and the Epic Games v. Apple fight over Fortnite (2020)
How an app works in simple terms: code, permissions and updates
keyFacts: Apple's App Store launched on July 10, 2008, with about 500 apps.
Android Market was renamed Google Play in March 2012.
M-Pesa launched in Kenya in 2007.
Today the major app stores each offer millions of apps.
outline.hook: End by zooming out from single apps to the whole planet: how did billions of phones change the way people live?

outline.title: A World in Your Pocket: How Smartphones Changed Society
covers: Scale: more than 4 billion people use a mobile phone to go online — more than half of humanity
Leapfrogging: many people in Africa and Asia skipped landline phones and desktop computers and went straight to mobile
Everyday life: maps instead of paper, video calls with faraway family, music and video streaming, online learning, banking
Work and the economy: new jobs (app makers, delivery and ride-hailing drivers), and work that follows you home
News and citizen journalism: ordinary people recording important events; phones in disasters and emergencies
Changes in how we communicate: emoji, selfies, group chats, social media
keyFacts: By the mid-2020s, more than 4 billion people used mobile internet.
There are more mobile phone subscriptions in the world than people.
M-Pesa grew to tens of millions of users across several African countries.
The word 'selfie' was chosen as Oxford Dictionaries' Word of the Year in 2013.
outline.hook: End with a fair warning: something this powerful also brings real problems — and Part 18 looks at them honestly.

outline.title: The Dark Side: Problems and Controversies
covers: Screen time, sleep and attention: why apps are designed to keep you scrolling; what research says and where scientists still disagree about mental health
Safety: distracted walking and texting while driving; cyberbullying and online strangers
Privacy: apps tracking location, data collection and advertising; security, scams and passwords
Phones in schools: many schools and some countries (for example France, from 2018) limit phones in class
Environment and people: rare and precious materials, cobalt mining in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (including child labor concerns), and e-waste
Repair and recycling: replaceable batteries, right-to-repair laws, and longer software updates
keyFacts: The world produced about 62 million tonnes of electronic waste in 2022, and less than a quarter was properly collected and recycled (UN Global E-waste Monitor 2024).
About 70% of the world's mined cobalt comes from the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
France passed a law in 2018 banning phone use in primary and middle schools.
In 2011 the WHO's cancer agency listed radio-frequency fields as 'possibly carcinogenic' (the same group as pickled vegetables) because evidence was limited, not because harm was proven.
outline.hook: End on hope: engineers and users are already working on better, safer, longer-lasting phones — which leads to what's next.

outline.title: Phones of Today and Tomorrow
covers: Folding phones: Royole FlexPai (2018), Samsung Galaxy Fold (2019, delayed after early screen problems), flip-style foldables
Satellite messaging: phones that can text emergency services from places with no cell signal (iPhone 14, 2022)
On-device artificial intelligence: voice assistants, live translation, photo editing, AI chips (NPUs)
Future networks (6G, expected around 2030), better batteries (such as solid-state batteries still in development), and augmented-reality glasses
Clearly label predictions as predictions; some may never happen
Will the smartphone itself be replaced — by wearables, glasses or something nobody has imagined yet?
keyFacts: Samsung's Galaxy Fold launched in September 2019 after being delayed from April.
Apple's Emergency SOS via satellite started with the iPhone 14 in 2022.
6G networks are being researched, with first launches commonly predicted around 2030.
Apple switched the iPhone to USB-C in 2023, partly because of the EU common-charger law.
outline.hook: End by inviting the reader to look back at the whole journey — from an 80-pound car phone to a phone that talks to satellites.

outline.title: From Brick to Brain: Putting It All Together
covers: A quick timeline recap: car phone (1946) → Cooper's call (1973) → first text (1992) → IBM Simon (1994) → BlackBerry (1999) → iPhone (2007) → Android (2008) → App Store (2008) → foldables and satellites
No single inventor: the smartphone combined dozens of inventions — radio, transistors, touchscreens, lithium-ion batteries, CMOS sensors, GPS, the internet
Lessons about invention: first is not always winner (Simon, Newton); timing and networks matter; giants can fall (Nokia, BlackBerry)
How small inventions add up: compare the DynaTAC and a modern phone (weight, talk time, abilities)
Using phones wisely: a balanced message about benefits and limits
Final challenge to the reader: what part of the phone would YOU reinvent?
keyFacts: The 1983 DynaTAC weighed about 790 g with 30 minutes of talk time; many modern smartphones weigh about 170–230 g and last a full day.
Fewer than 40 years passed between the first handheld cellular call (1973) and billions of smartphones (2010s).
Billions of smartphones are now in use worldwide.
The smartphone depends on Nobel Prize–winning science, including transistors, CCD image sensors and lithium-ion batteries.
outline.hook: Close the whole Deep Dive with an inspiring final line about the next inventor maybe being the reader.

glossary: cellular network — a phone network that divides land into small areas called cells, each with its own tower, so radio channels can be reused
cell tower (base station) — an antenna and radio equipment that connects phones in one cell to the rest of the network
handoff — passing a call or data connection from one cell tower to the next as you move
analog vs digital — analog sends a smooth wave copying the sound; digital turns it into numbers (1s and 0s)
1G / 2G / 3G / 4G / 5G — generations of mobile networks; each newer one is faster and can carry more data
SMS — short message service: text messages of up to 160 characters
SIM card — a small chip card that identifies your phone account to the network
PDA — personal digital assistant: a handheld electronic organizer, usually without a phone
smartphone — a mobile phone that is also a general-purpose computer able to run apps and use the internet
operating system (OS) — the main software that runs a phone and its apps, such as Android or iOS
app — an application: a program you install on a phone to do a particular job
capacitive touchscreen — a screen that senses your finger by the tiny change it makes in an electric field
resistive touchscreen — a screen that senses where two flexible layers are pressed together
multi-touch — a touchscreen's ability to sense two or more touches at once, allowing gestures like pinch-to-zoom
transistor — a tiny electronic switch; billions of them make up a phone's chip
system-on-a-chip (SoC) — one chip that holds the processor, graphics, AI engine, modem and more
lithium-ion battery — a rechargeable battery in which lithium ions move between two electrodes
image sensor (CMOS) — the chip in a camera that turns light into electrical signals, pixel by pixel
GPS — Global Positioning System: US satellites whose signals let a receiver work out its location
accelerometer — a sensor that measures movement and tilt, for example to rotate the screen
doNotSay: Do not say Steve Jobs or Apple invented the smartphone — the iPhone (2007) came after IBM Simon, Nokia Communicators, BlackBerry, Palm Treo and others; it popularized the modern touchscreen smartphone.
Do not say Alexander Graham Bell invented the mobile or cell phone.
Do not say Martin Cooper invented the phone alone or that cellular networks were his idea — the cell concept came from Bell Labs (1947) and many engineers at Motorola and Bell Labs contributed.
Do not state as fact that Star Trek inspired Cooper's phone — Cooper has told different versions (he has also mentioned Dick Tracy); present it as his own later recollection.
Do not say the IBM Simon was called a 'smartphone' when it was sold — the label was applied later.
Do not say the first iPhone had an App Store, 3G, or video recording — it had none of these.
Do not say Google invented Android from scratch — it began as the startup Android Inc., which Google bought in 2005.
Do not say Gorilla Glass was invented for the iPhone — it came from Corning's 1960s Chemcor research.
Do not say Hedy Lamarr invented Wi-Fi, Bluetooth or GPS — she co-patented a frequency-hopping idea related to later spread-spectrum technologies.
Do not say Shigetaka Kurita created the very first emoji — J-Phone had an earlier set in 1997; Kurita's 1999 set was highly influential.
Do not say phone radiation is proven to cause cancer — large studies have not shown that; the WHO agency's 'possibly carcinogenic' label (2011) reflects limited evidence.
Do not say smartphones are scientifically proven to cause depression in all teens — research shows links and concerns but scientists still debate cause and effect.
Do not say more megapixels always means better photos.
Do not say charging overnight or leaving a phone at 100% will quickly destroy the battery, or that phones commonly explode — battery fires are rare.
Do not say the first text message was sent from one phone to another — it was sent from a computer to a phone.
Do not say phones are millions of times 'smarter' than Apollo-era computers in a vague way — compare specific numbers like memory or speed.
Do not say the Nokia 3310 was indestructible or unbreakable — it was tough, but that is a joke/meme.
Do not say 1G phones were digital or that the 1946 car phone was cellular.
